FlowBus Demo Guide
Pick the problem you want to solve first
Each entry point demonstrates only one capability. Clicking on it and performing an action allows you to quickly understand how to use the module.
What this is: a question-driven demo guide. You do not need to memorize names like `postEvent`, `sticky`, or `eventChannel` before getting started.
When to use it: when you are new to this library, or when you want to quickly confirm which kind of messaging fits your current scenario.
What this page shows: the 6 entries below map to 6 common questions. Pick the one that sounds most like your situation, then open the single-purpose case page.
Choose by scenario
Each page explains only one thing: what it is, when to use it, what one action will show you, the smallest useful code, and what not to do.

Global event case
When should you notify the whole app with a global event?
This page demonstrates the most typical broadcast scenario: one action happens, then other pages or modules can receive the same refresh signal.
What this is: a global broadcast notification sent by `postEvent` and collected by `eventFlow`.
When to use it: when different pages, modules, or owners should all know that the same change has happened, such as a successful login refreshing the home page.
What this page shows: tap once and compare what the sender did with what the receiver got, so the send -> receive chain of a global broadcast becomes obvious.

Smallest useful code
postEvent(GlobalEvent("login-success"))
collectEvent(eventFlow<GlobalEvent>()) { event ->
 render(event.message)
}
Do not use this first when only the current page needs a refresh, or when the message should stay inside the current Activity / Fragment. That makes the scope too large too early.
Decision guide
Which one should I use?
This page is static on purpose. It helps you map common questions to the recommended API without extra interaction.

Remember one rule first: keep the scope as small as possible. If it can stay in the current owner, do not make it global. If you need replay of the latest state, then consider Sticky. If the payload type is the same but meanings differ, consider eventChannel.
Different pages or modules all need to know about the same change
Recommended: `postEvent` + `eventFlow`. Good for login success, global config changes, and app-wide refresh signals.
Only the current Activity owner or current Fragment should receive it
Recommended: `postScopedEvent` + `scopedEventFlow`. Good for local UI refreshes that should not leak into the whole app.
The current page needs the latest state again after recreation
Recommended: `postScopedStickyEvent` + `scopedStickyEventFlow`. The key idea is replay inside the same owner, not permanent storage across a brand-new owner.
The payload type is the same, but the business meaning is totally different
Recommended: `eventChannel(\"name\")` + `channel.flow()`. Good for things like toast messages, navigation commands, and page-only tips that all use `String` but must never mix.
The sender should not depend on the page directly
Recommended: treat the event bus as a decoupled notification path so ViewModel, Repository, and Worker can notify without holding page references.
Sticky supplementary case
How does Sticky replay the latest state after the current page is recreated?

This page focuses on Sticky replay inside the current Activity owner. First remember the latest toolbar state, then recreate the current page and watch the new page instance receive that latest state automatically.
What this is: replay of the latest state inside the current `Activity owner`. It is not a normal event, and it is not permanent storage across a brand-new page.
When to use it: when the current page should still get the latest state after recreation, such as restoring the latest toolbar state.
What this page shows: remember one state, recreate the current page, then watch the new page instance replay the latest Sticky state automatically.

Smallest useful code
postScopedStickyEvent(ActivityEvent("toolbar-ready"))
collectEvent(scopedStickyEventFlow<ActivityEvent>()) { event ->
 render(event.message)
}
Do not use this when your real target is opening a brand-new Activity and inheriting the old page state. Scoped Sticky lives on the current owner, so a new owner means a new boundary.

eventChannel case
This page shows how the same String payload can be separated into different business channels instead of being mixed together.
Use different named channels when the payload type is the same but the business meaning is different.
Why introduce channels when everything is still a String?
This case separates toast, navigation, and page-only tips. The payload type stays the same, but the business meaning no longer gets mixed together.
What this is: giving the same payload type different channel names, so subscribers listen by business meaning instead of mixing everything because it is all `String`.
When to use it: when toast messages, navigation commands, and page-only tips share the same data shape but must never flow through the same stream.
What this page shows: tap different buttons and only the matching result area updates, so the boundary of “same type, different channel” is obvious.
Predefined channels
`ui.toast` is for one-shot feedback, `ui.navigation` is for route commands, and `ui.snackbar` is for page-only tips.

If you only use raw String events, toast, navigation, and page tips are easy to mix together. Named channels keep the type the same while separating intent.

Do not throw toast messages, navigation commands, and page tips into one raw String event just because it feels faster today. The moment receivers grow, the branching logic becomes messy and meanings start to leak together.
Non-UI flow
This case shows how ViewModel, Repository, and Worker can notify the page without calling the page directly.
This demo is about decoupled notifications. It is not asking you to replace normal function calls with an event bus.
Why can ViewModel, Repository, and Worker notify UI without depending on the page?
Tap once to start a sync flow, then watch ViewModel, Repository, and Worker emit logs separately while the page only listens for notifications.
What this is: a decoupled notification path where senders do not hold page references and only publish notifications.
When to use it: when ViewModel, Repository, or Worker finishes background work and the page is only one possible receiver of that notification.
What this page shows: tap once, then watch the ViewModel, Repository, and Worker logs light up in sequence before the page renders the final result.

Smallest useful code
viewModel.runNonUiDemo()
DefaultFlowBus.flow<WorkerDemoLog>().collect { event ->
 render(event.message)
}
Do not use the event bus to replace normal return values, repository calls, or request-response flows. Use it for notifications, not as a default transport for everything.
Scoped communication case
Why should some messages stay inside the current owner?
This page shows what belongs to the current Activity owner, what stays inside the current Fragment, and why you should not start with global events for local UI refreshes.
What this is: local communication constrained to the current `Activity owner` or current `Fragment`, so it does not become an app-wide broadcast.
When to use it: when an action only affects the current host, current panel, or current owner, and you want the notification boundary to stay local.
What this page shows: first the current Activity refreshes itself, then the current Fragment either refreshes only itself or sends a targeted local message back to the host.
Host area: current Activity
Use this button when the current Activity needs a local refresh. The result area below tells you who received the message and who did not.

Smallest useful code
postScopedEvent(ActivityEvent("toolbar-refresh"))
collectEvent(scopedEventFlow<ActivityEvent>()) { event ->
 render(event.message)
}
Do not turn a local UI refresh into a global event just because it works quickly. That makes the boundary too wide and hides who really needs to receive the message.
